brief: A tool caddy with a carry handle and divided bins for screws and bits.

requirements.requirement: Tool caddy (one unit you can carry)
requirements.evidence: 3 full bases (piece:-1,0,0, 0,0,0, 1,0,0) joined in a row by 2 joint bolts, with all open faces capped

handle:0,0,0;top is fitted on cover:0,0,0;full;top over the middle cell, centred between the two bins. The configurator checks fit only, so it can't say whether the handle is strong enough to carry a loaded caddy.
bin:-1,0,0~hex-bin-full-div3 has 3 compartments holding screws, nuts and standoffs
bin:1,0,0~hex-bin-full-div2 has 2 compartments. The props show screws in one and a standing hex driver in the other, because the catalogue has no prop for loose bits.

finish.summary: I built a 3-cell tool caddy in a straight row. The middle cell has a top cover with a carry handle. The left cell holds a full-depth bin with 3 compartments and the right cell a full-depth bin with 2 compartments. I put end caps on all open faces and bolted the joints together. I filled the bins with sample props: screws, nuts and standoffs on the left, screws and a standing hex driver on the right. The props sit below the bin rims, so you see them from above, not from the side. check_build passed with no issues and the parts don't collide. The design has 30 parts and needs about 1628 g of filament and about 2310 minutes to print.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
